title: Hashes
subtitle: HSET, HGET, HMGET, and efficient object storage
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: Storing structured objects as a single JSON string means deserializing the whole object just to read or update one field. Storing each field as a separate string key creates key sprawl and multiple round-trips.
whyItExists.solution: Redis Hashes store field-value pairs under one key. You can get/set individual fields in O(1) without deserializing the whole object. They use a compact in-memory format for small objects.
whyItExists.whenToUse: User profiles, session data, product details, counters grouped by entity — any time you have an object with known fields that you read/update partially.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: If you need TTL per field (not supported), or if the object has nested structures (use JSON strings or RedisJSON). Hashes also can't be queried by field value.

explainModes.beginner: A Hash in Redis is like a drawer with labeled compartments. The drawer has a name (the key), and inside are labeled slots (fields) each holding a value. You can open one compartment without emptying the whole drawer.
explainModes.simple: HSET stores field-value pairs under one key. HGET reads one field. HMGET reads multiple fields in one call. HGETALL reads everything. HINCRBY atomically increments a numeric field without reading it first.
explainModes.standard: Redis Hashes map string fields to string values. All hash commands are prefixed with H. HSET is O(1) per field. HGETALL is O(N) in the number of fields. Use HMGET to fetch multiple fields in one round-trip. HINCRBY and HINCRBYFLOAT provide atomic increments without GET/SET cycles.
explainModes.technical: Redis encodes small hashes as a listpack (compact flat array) when field count ≤ hash-max-listpack-entries (default 128) and all values are ≤ hash-max-listpack-value (default 64 bytes). Above those thresholds, it converts to a hash table. Listpack is 3-5x more memory-efficient. HRANDFIELD (Redis 6.2+) returns random fields, useful for sampling.
explainModes.deepDive: The listpack encoding stores fields and values as inline entries: [prevlen][len][data]. This is cache-line friendly for small hashes. The conversion from listpack to hash table is one-way and triggered by any single field exceeding the threshold. For large objects, consider using GET/SET with JSON + RedisJSON module for nested access and partial update with JSONPath. Hash expiry per field (HEXPIRE) was added in Redis 7.4.

content.text: Hashes store field-value pairs under a single key — like a mini-document. They're perfect for user profiles, session data, and product records where you want to read or update individual fields without loading the whole object.

content.code:
# Store an object
HSET user:1 name "Alice" email "alice@example.com" age 30 city "London"

# Read one field
HGET user:1 name         # "Alice"

# Read multiple fields in one round-trip
HMGET user:1 name email  # ["Alice", "alice@example.com"]

# Read all fields
HGETALL user:1
# 1) "name"
# 2) "Alice"
# 3) "email"
# 4) "alice@example.com"
# ...

# Check field existence
HEXISTS user:1 email  # 1
HEXISTS user:1 phone  # 0

# Count fields
HLEN user:1  # 4

# Update one field without touching others
HSET user:1 city "Paris"

# Delete a field
HDEL user:1 phone

# Atomic increment of a numeric field
HSET user:1 loginCount 0
HINCRBY user:1 loginCount 1    # 1
HINCRBY user:1 loginCount 1    # 2
HINCRBYFLOAT user:1 score 1.5  # floating point increment

# Set field only if not exists
HSETNX user:1 role "admin"  # only sets if 'role' field doesn't exist

# Get all keys or values
HKEYS user:1   # ["name", "email", "age", "city"]
HVALS user:1   # ["Alice", "alice@example.com", "30", "Paris"]

content.text: Hashes are ideal for session storage. You can update individual session fields (like last activity) without reading and rewriting the entire session object.

content.title: Hash vs JSON String for Objects

a.name: Redis Hash
strengths: Update single fields without full read/write
a.useWhen: Objects with known flat fields that need partial updates

b.name: JSON String (GET/SET)
weaknesses: Deserialize whole object for one field
b.useWhen: Complex nested objects, or when you always read/write the whole object

content.text: Use HMGET instead of multiple HGET calls to fetch several fields in one network round-trip. For reading the entire object, HGETALL is equivalent but returns all fields — be cautious on large hashes.
Avoid very large hashes (thousands of fields). For user activity logs or large datasets, use separate keys or Redis Streams instead.

questions.question: What command retrieves all fields and values from a Redis hash?
questions.explanation: HGETALL returns all field-value pairs. Use HSCAN for large hashes to avoid blocking on iteration.

questions.question: How do you atomically increment a numeric field in a hash?
options: GET field, increment in app, SET field
questions.explanation: HINCRBY increments a hash field's integer value atomically. HINCRBYFLOAT does the same for floats. No GET/SET round-trip needed — the increment is atomic.

questions.question: What encoding does Redis use for small hashes?
questions.explanation: Small hashes (default ≤128 fields, ≤64 bytes/value) use a listpack encoding — a compact flat byte array that is 3-5x more memory-efficient than a hash table.

faq.q: How many fields can a Redis hash have?
faq.a: Up to 2^32 - 1 (over 4 billion) fields. In practice, keep hashes small and focused — large hashes with thousands of fields are better split across multiple keys.

faq.q: Can I expire a single hash field?
faq.a: Redis 7.4 added HEXPIRE for field-level expiry, but it's not yet available on all managed services. For older versions, use separate string keys if you need per-field TTL.
HSCAN iterates over hash fields in cursor-based batches without blocking. Use it instead of HGETALL on very large hashes to avoid a single O(N) blocking operation.
